items.q: When can I sign up for health insurance?
items.a: For ACA plans, during the annual Open Enrollment Period. For 2027 coverage on HealthCare.gov it runs November 1, 2026 through January 15, 2027; enroll by December 15 for coverage starting January 1. State-run marketplaces can have different deadlines. Outside Open Enrollment you need a Special Enrollment Period. See the open enrollment guide.

items.q: What is a Special Enrollment Period?
items.a: A window, usually 60 days, to enroll in or change a Marketplace plan after a qualifying life event such as losing other health coverage, moving to a new area, getting married, having or adopting a child, or certain changes in income. You may be asked to show documents proving the event.

items.q: Can I sign up for Medicaid or CHIP any time?
items.a: Yes. Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program accept applications all year. Eligibility depends on your state, household size and income.

items.q: I just lost my job. What should I do first?
items.a: Don’t wait. Losing job-based coverage generally gives you 60 days to pick a Marketplace plan, and you’ll also be offered COBRA if your employer is large enough. Compare both before the window closes; see COBRA alternatives.

items.q: What’s the difference between a premium, deductible, copay and out-of-pocket maximum?
items.a: The premium is what you pay each month to keep coverage. The deductible is what you pay for covered care before the plan starts sharing costs (preventive care is often covered before it). Copays and coinsurance are your share after that. The out-of-pocket maximum is the most you’ll pay for covered in-network care in a plan year; after that, the plan pays 100%.

items.q: Will I qualify for help paying my premium?
items.a: Marketplace premium tax credits are based on household income and size, and on whether you can get affordable job-based coverage. For 2026 and later they’re generally available from 100% to 400% of the federal poverty level, since the enhanced credits of 2021–2025 expired. Joe can help you estimate based on your situation.

items.q: Does using an agent cost me more?
items.a: No. For the same plan, the premium is the same whether you buy it yourself or through a licensed agent. Agents are typically paid a commission by the insurance company. {{todo:Joe to confirm compensation disclosure wording.}}

items.q: What’s the difference between a PPO, HMO and EPO?
items.a: HMOs usually require you to use in-network doctors and get referrals to see specialists. EPOs also limit you to the network (except emergencies) but usually don’t need referrals. PPOs let you see out-of-network providers at a higher cost. See PPO vs. HMO vs. EPO.

On ACA-compliant plans, yes. They can’t deny you, exclude a condition or charge more because of your health. Non-ACA products such as short-term and medically underwritten plans can. See ACA vs. private health insurance.

Only if your doctor is in the plan’s network (or the plan covers out-of-network care). Before you enroll, check each doctor, your hospital and your prescriptions against the plan’s directory and drug list.

items.q: Can I stay on my parent’s plan?
items.a: Yes, until you turn 26, if the plan offers dependent coverage. See turning 26.

items.q: How does a quote with Joe work?
items.a: Call {{phone}} or book a time. Joe will ask about your household, income range, doctors and prescriptions, then walk you through the options that fit. There’s no obligation to buy.

items.q: Is this website affiliated with HealthCare.gov or the government?
items.a: No. Insurance Guy Joe is a private insurance agency and isn’t affiliated with HealthCare.gov, any state marketplace, Medicare or any government agency. See our disclaimers.
